contentText:
"Rinku, what about our Iceland trip?" I questioned, sipping on Old Monk during a laid-back weekend getaway near Chikmagalur. 
 
 Rinku, deep in thought, replied, “Not sure… I’m planning a career switch. If things settle down by December, maybe we can go in late January for yours and Harini’s birthday—or the first week of February.” I wasn’t entirely convinced. With 14 leaves about to lapse, I was eager to make it happen this year itself. If we postponed now, it would be the second time. This trip had  to happen this year. Luck, however, had other plans. Rinku secured a fantastic job, and just like that, we were set to hit the Icy road for Iceland! 
 01/12/2024 - The Journey Begins 
 As expected, the drama began early. At Frankfurt, Germany, we were denied boarding for our connecting flight to Reykjavik— despite  being at the gate on time. The delay from our Bangalore-to-Frankfurt flight had caused chaos, and to make things worse, Lufthansa overbooked the flight. Their customer service? Absolutely pathetic. Four hours of standing in a never-moving queue for rebooking, without so much as a courtesy call to inform us or offer an alternative. Classic Lufthansa, right? Eventually, after what felt like an eternity, we got rebooked—via Sweden—to Reykjavik. By the time we arrived at Reykjavik Airport, it was close to midnight. Exhausted and freezing, we discovered that our self-drive rental had been cancelled  due to the late arrival. 
 After some scrambling, we managed to strike a direct deal with the same provider. Same cost, but 50 euros extra for late-night pickup. Considering the circumstances, we took it. “Looks pretty neat,” I mumbled through chattering teeth, taking a quick look at our Vitara Brezza in the dim airport light. The car seemed ready for the adventure ahead—if only we were too. We drove straight to our Airbnb and collapsed into bed, knowing we had a couple of hours of driving to do the next morning. 02/12/2024 - A Windy Affair with Snæfellsnes I woke up thinking it was too early—the sky was still blanketed in darkness. Just as I started to roll over,  Rinku’s voice, “Macha, we’re late for breakfast. Let’s go!”. It was 8:30 AM, and I hadn’t even realized it. Iceland’s winter darkness had already messed with my sense of time. We quickly freshened up, excitement bubbling as the thought of starting our road trip sank in. However with a slight doubt —could we make it through Snæfellsnes before the yellow weather alerts kicked in post-lunch? After savouring our complimentary English breakfast, we loaded the car and hit the road towards the Snæfellsnes Peninsula. We were en route to our first destination— Ytri Tunga Beach —to spot some seals. Seals, Wind, and (Mild) Chaos “It’s too cold to even step out!”  the girls complained as they opened the car doors, bracing against the biting winter wind. Well, it was Iceland in December—what else could we expect? We started walking towards the beach, reading the signboards that reminded us to keep a respectful distance from the shore and to stay quiet to avoid disturbing the seals. “Look at that shoal of seals!”, suddenly, someone pointed. We turned to see a group of seals swimming about 300 meters away. Though our lenses couldn’t capture much, our eyes did, and it was a memory worth keeping. Further along the shore, a lone seal was sprawled lazily on a rock, upside down.  “That seal reminded me of my wife!” 😂 The Overrated (but Beautiful) Black Church 
 Our next stop was the Black Church at Búðir . A stark contrast of black against white snowy landscapes, the church is small but undeniably charming. While it lacks the grandeur of European cathedrals, its uniqueness lies in its simplicity. “Do you know why it’s black?” I asked. 
 “Black absorbs everything, right? Isn’t that counterproductive in the cold?   ”Rinku shrugged. 
 “No idea. Let’s move before we freeze. ” By 2 PM, the girls declared it was lunchtime. Unfortunately, we hadn’t packed lunch due to the previous day’s flight delays, so we decided to grab something en route. Finding a restaurant in Iceland during winter feels like finding logic in my friend group—rare and improbable. But we managed to spot one, thanks to a helpful signboard directing us to take a detour. “I’ll have to sell my kidney to finish this trip,” I exclaimed, staring at the prices. A burger and two mini fries set us back a whopping 5,200 ISK. Yes, Iceland is expensive—everything is imported—but the quality and hygiene are top-notch. Battling the Yellow Alert “Macha, the yellow alert has started. Should we keep driving?” Rinku asked, concerned. 
 “No way we’re turning back,” I replied, firm but slightly sceptical. We had never experienced Iceland’s infamous storms, and I wasn’t sure how bad it could get. After checking alternate routes, we found one road already closed due to winds. The other two were passable—one longer and one shorter. Our planned route was the longer one, as we had hoped to catch the sunset at Djúpalónssandur , the Black Sand Beach. In Iceland, sunsets are a rarity, as the skies are often overcast. Still, we decided to risk it. Iceland’s winters are bearable, but the winds are what make it brutal. By the time we reached Djúpalónssandur, the winds were no joke. As I stretched to wear my jacket, the gusts pushed me backwards, jacket and all. Iceland’s winds are a force to be reckoned with—more chilling than the winter cold itself. We couldn’t get past the parking area, but that didn’t stop Rinku, Cutti, and me from having fun. We jumped and played, letting the winds toss us around like kids rediscovering their innocence. “You guys are such kids,” muttered Farini, shivering as she slammed the car door shut. The Yellow Alert - Strong winds by picking up the ice After braving the winds, we made it to our cozy B&B for the night. It was warm, welcoming, and exactly what we needed. We prepared tasty biryani and wrapped our day. Snæfellsnes had given us its best—and its worst—but it was all part of the adventure we’d come for. 
 3/12/2024 - Kirkjufell, Lava Falls & A Love Book Surprise Our third day in Iceland, and the excitement still hadn’t faded. We were finally going to visit Kirkjufell , the iconic cone-shaped mountain that seemed to be plastered across every Iceland travel blog. “I still don’t get why this is so hyped,” I muttered to myself while scrolling through yet another blog post about it. Maybe it was the shape, maybe the surrounding landscape. From our Airbnb’s living room, the view was spectacular. Kirkjufell stood majestically, framed by the crisp winter air and the first light of the day. It was that  close. 
 While breakfast was being prepared, I grabbed a coffee and flipped through the magazines stacked on the table. One book caught my attention— “Love.” Curious, I randomly opened a page. My eyes opened wide. Right there, a couple was in an intimate position—Missionary. I turned the page. Next up—Cowgirl. “Wait, what kind of book is this?!” 
 Excited, I called my wife and friends over. 
 “You pervert!” Farini snapped, walking away. I turned another page, expecting more… but what I saw next threw me off completely—a toddler playing with a dog. The next page? A rustic mother and son standing in a farm field. “Oh damn… This book isn’t about that  kind of love… It’s about all  forms of love.” I stared at it for a second, processing my newfound enlightenment. I turned to Cutti and the others. “Wow. Happy realisation,” my wife said. Farini, still unimpressed, threw in some sarcasm. And with that, we packed our bags, spun the wheel, and set off towards Kirkjufell . Kirkjufell & The Drive to Hraunfossar 
 As expected, it was freezing outside, but the view made up for it. Kirkjufell stood tall, its conical peak contrasting beautifully against the sky, with Kirkjufellsfoss  flowing gracefully opposite to it. Happy us @ Kirkjufell For context—foss means waterfall in Icelandic. This one? Small, cute… kinda like my wife. 😛 After soaking in the view, we continued towards Hraunfossar , also known as Lava Falls . The drive itself was breathtaking—everywhere we looked, the landscape screamed wow, wow, and wow. We finally reached the falls, and let me tell you—this was something else. The waterfalls stretched across hundreds of meters, with ice creeping in from the edges but not fully freezing over. Water still trickled through various channels, creating a mesmerizing effect. 
 A kind lady who offered to take our pictures casually explained, “This waterfall formed when lava caves collapsed after an eruption long ago.” I nodded, pretending I knew exactly  when that happened. 😛 By the time we checked the clock, it was already 4 PM—and we still hadn’t eaten. Starving, we hurried back to the car park to dig into our very  frozen packed lunch. Thankfully, we had hot chocolate to go with it, because the café had a buy something or no washroom  policy. Fun fact: Most public washrooms in Iceland are free, but some places make you purchase something before you can access them. Rare, but it happens. With daylight gone, we started our drive back to Reykjavik, passing through the Hvalfjörður Tunnel —an absolute monster at 5,800 meters . “This is ducking long,” I muttered, genuinely impressed. After reaching Reykjavik, we checked into Dalur - Hi Eco Hostel . 
 This place was awesome, keypad-secured doors for both the hostel entrance and the rooms, all automated. No human interaction—just an email with our booking details and PIN codes. Efficient, yet slightly annoying in case if we need something. The kitchen? A dream. Every appliance you could ask for, ready to go. We ended the night with a true  comfort meal— Plain white rice, Steaming hot rasam, Chutney pudi, and Beer.  Oh, and of course, curd—because what kind of South Indian would I be without it? 
 
 We installed Hello Aurora , an aurora spotting app, which provides real-time updates on aurora activity levels and visibility. Although there wasn’t much activity forecasted for that night, we decided to give it one last hopeful try. We drove to the edge of Reykjavik, to the Grotta Island Lighthouse , a popular northern lights viewing spot. As we reached, the temperature plummeted and it was biting  cold. Despite shivering and hopping in and out of the car like confused penguins, we waited patiently, eyes scanning the horizon. An hour passed… and nothing. No sign of the lights, no colours in the sky—just the howling wind and the freezing air. Finally, we gave up and decided to head back to the hostel to sleep. 
 And just like that, another day in Iceland came to a close. 04/12/2024 - The Land of Ice, Fire & Cutti’s Ice-Skating Stunt The morning was chilled, quite literally, but there wasn’t much rush to start our day. Still, we had to move quickly—daylight in Iceland is as rare as a budget-friendly meal here. After a quick breakfast at the hostel, we packed up and checked out, making our way to Bónus , the go-to supermarket in Reykjavik. This was our last stop in the city for the next four days, so we had to stock up on essentials. Supermarkets in Reykjavik? Cheap and convenient.
Supermarkets in other parts of Iceland? Uncommon. 
Also, most shut early in the evening. We grabbed everything we could—fruits, berries, cookies, chocolates—and hit the road towards our next stop: Geysir. Ever since I saw a video of a geyser erupting on a fellow traveller’s phone back at our Airbnb, I had been buzzing with excitement. Seeing it in real life? That was a whole other level. As we parked and walked towards the geothermal area, we could literally feel  the heat beneath our feet. The contrast was insane—freezing cold air, yet steaming ground. 
 Along the path, we passed small boiling ponds, their surfaces bubbling aggressively like a giant’s cauldron. “Good thing there’s a caution board,” my brain noted, silently appreciating that Iceland doesn’t believe in natural selection. Finally, we reached the Great Geysir.  The pool itself wasn’t huge—about the size of a traditional well—but the anticipation was real. The water boiled continuously, simmering for a few minutes before… BOOM!  A massive jet of scalding water shot 10-15 feet into the air, creating a surreal spectacle. The cycle is repeated every few minutes—boil, build-up, explosion, cooldown, repeat. An absolute marvel of nature. The Geysir Iceland truly lives up to its title—the land of ice and fire. To warm ourselves up, we grabbed some hot chocolate from a restaurant near the parking lot—a small but delicious bonus. Gullfoss - The Golden Falls & Cutti’s Slip of Fate Next up— Gullfoss , aka the Golden Falls . Some legends say Vikings threw gold into the waters, giving it its name. I say it’s just an expensive  looking waterfall. The moment we stepped out of the car, Cutti’s words summed up the situation perfectly—“Ah, it’s so freezing cold,” she stammered, struggling to walk as sudden gusts of wind made the already chilling temperatures even worse. As I stood there, soaking in the beauty, I suddenly heard— Thuddddd! I turned around to see Cutti lying flat on the ice, looking very  betrayed by the ground. Damn my thoughts—I was just admiring the beauty of the place, and the universe immediately struck her with Nazar. Luckily, aside from a bruised right hand, she was fine. 
 Off to Flúðir - The Coziest Wrap to the Day Instead of driving back to Reykjavik to start our journey towards Jökulsárlón , we took a more direct route and booked a private cabin in Flúðir  for the night. And wow—what a place. Cozy wooden interiors, a huge TV, and a perfect setting to wind down. We cooked some noodles, cracked open some beers, and tuned into Netflix. The movie of the night? "Lucky Bhaskar"—because nothing says adventure like a Telugu movie in the middle of Iceland. 
 The Mild Aurora - View from our Airbnb And just like that, another epic day came to an end. 05/12/2024 - A Day of Frozen Falls & Nearly Getting Blown Away The previous night, we discovered that Sky Lagoon  was just a mile away from our stay. “Of course, why would we miss dipping ourselves in a thermal pool?” Rinku declared, making it clear that this would be the first thing we did today. Waking up early in Iceland is a challenge—especially when the bed is warm, and the outside world is freezing. But by 7 AM, we were up, prepping breakfast and packing lunch to ensure we made it to the lagoon early, avoiding the crowds. Luckily, when we reached, the place was almost  empty—just around ten people in the entire pool. We quickly changed into our swimwear and took a dip. “Ooohhhh it’s cold!” the girls shrieked as they ran through the icy air toward the pool. But the moment we got in, the magic of Iceland’s geothermal waters took over. Sky lagoon Thermal pools are one of Iceland’s biggest treasures. Sky Lagoon is no exception—a huge 100x100 pond filled with natural hot water drawn from underground. Since the water at the source is around 100 degrees Celsius, it’s mixed with cold water before being routed to the pool, making it just perfect  for soaking in. Smiles after a steamy hot bath amidst of teeth-biting cold After a blissful dip, we grabbed some breakfast and hit the road towards the waterfalls of the day. Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi - The Frozen Beauties Today was all about frozen waterfalls —and the first on our list was Seljalandsfoss , a towering cascade that crashes down from over 100 feet. You can feel the mist on your face even from a distance . As we admired the fall, Farini suddenly shoved her phone in my face. “Balu, look at this! It’s amazing! Why aren’t we going here?”  she demanded, showing me an Instagram reel of another stunning waterfall. 
 
 I sighed. This is why people should check the itinerary. 
 “Huh, that’s literally our next stop— Gljúfrabúi ,” I replied, dripping with sarcasm. 
 
 “Okay fineeee,” she muttered in her classic mocking tone. 
 Gljúfrabúi  is lesser-known but equally breathtaking—a partially frozen waterfall hidden inside a narrow canyon. What we didn’t  know? It was just a short walk from Seljalandsfoss. Instead of walking, we blindly followed Google Maps… which led us straight to a private property with a huge “NO ENTRY” sign. “Nice. Now what?” Rinku sighed. 
  We turned back, defeated, only to spot people walking towards the falls. 
 “There, there! People are walking!” I pointed excitedly. Rinku quickly parked, and we joined the group. As we stepped onto the narrow, icy path, the sheer beauty of Gljúfrabúi hit us. The falls were hidden behind a rocky entrance, making the experience even more surreal. 
 The only downside? The path was super slippery, and at some points, we had to step into freezing water. Rinku, being the genius that he is, had forgotten his gloves. Holding onto the icy boulders for balance? Not fun. Within minutes, his hands turned numb, forcing him to run back Skógafoss - The Grand Finale of Waterfalls After our icy adventure, we continued towards Vik , where we had booked our next stay. But before that, one last stop— Skógafoss . And let me just say—this waterfall is 100/10. It’s similar in height to Seljalandsfoss, but way wider, making it even more dramatic. The best part? The partially frozen ice leading up to it, where you could literally  see water flowing beneath the fresh ice sheet. I now understood the quote “the journey is more beautiful than the destination.” Of course, we had to trouble a photographer nearby to get some decent pictures. “Macha, let’s move. It’s already past sunset,” Rinku reminded us, snapping us out of our waterfall trance. We had 90 minutes to reach our Airbnb and started driving towards Vik. The Airbnb Disaster & The Night We Almost Got Blown Away After a long drive, we finally arrived at Kirkjubæjarklaustur , a small village between Vik and Hofn. “Where’s our stay?” Rinku asked, frowning at the lack of, well… anything. 
 “I don’t know. This is where the Airbnb location ended,” I replied, equally confused. I opened the Airbnb to read this message from the host “Please don’t follow the Airbnb location. Our actual place is 30 km away. Here’s the real landmark.” 30. Freaking. Kilometers. Behind.
I was pissed. Who even uploads the wrong location on Airbnb?! What an ass! As we sat there fuming, the winds suddenly picked up. Hard. The car started shaking violently. Yellow alert. For a moment, I genuinely wondered if we’d get blown away . Luckily, we had four heavy asses inside and a trunk full of luggage anchoring us down. 😂 
 At this point, I wasn’t in the mood to drive back. I called Airbnb, got the booking cancelled, and they suggested a new stay— Bikers Farm Iceland. 
 In my frustration, I booked it without reading the description. Bad move. As we reached, the winds had only gotten worse—Rinku, carrying three bags, nearly got blown off his feet. That’s how strong it was.  Then came another surprise—the kitchen and bathrooms were separate from the rooms, meaning we had to walk 50 meters through deadly winds just to pee, and to make things worse, the heater was small, barely functional for Iceland’s brutal cold. At this point, we were too tired and somehow managed to sleep through the chaos.  The only best part of the day? A good tummy full of spicy noodles and a beer.  Also, nobody woke me and Rinku up for a bathroom run. 
 And with that, another legendary day in Iceland came to a close. 06/12/2024 - Walking on Ice, Chasing Lights & Parking Disaster This was it—the day we had been waiting for. The Skaftafell Ice Cave & Glacier Hike  was finally happening. We reached Arctic Adventures at 9:10 AM, a good ten minutes late. Typical. If there’s one thing we Indians need to work on, it’s arriving on time . We were the last ones to reach, but thankfully, the guides were still helping others gear up. We quickly filled out safety forms, strapped on our helmets, and grabbed our ice axes—because, of course, what’s a glacier hike without feeling like a Viking? A van took us to the starting point of the Vatnajökull Glacier , the largest in Iceland, covering 15% of the country . Yeah, it’s that  massive. The Glacier That Wasn’t Black—It Was Just Covered in Sand After a short walk, we stopped to put on our crampons, and the real hike began. At first, the trail looked completely black, and we assumed we’d see the glacier after this stretch. But nope—the trail itself was a glacier, just covered in black volcanic ash. As we walked, our crampons scraped the surface, revealing the pure ice underneath. d Walking on a glacier—wowww. One of the coolest (literally) things I’ve done. Then, up ahead, we saw it—a massive, crystal-clear glacier wall, stretching so high it seemed to touch the sky, like an ocean frozen in time. 
 The sun was just rising over the horizon, casting a golden glow over the icy landscape. The sky turned into a breathtaking mix of orange and blue hues, making the whole experience unreal The Blue Ice Cave & Farini’s Phone Tragedy After a solid trek, we finally reached the Blue Ice Cave . The cave is semi-natural—guides check it daily and carve a path if needed since glaciers constantly move, albeit at a tortoise’s pace. The entrance was a narrow passage, allowing only one person at a time. Walking inside was surreal—the ice had trapped bubbles due to pressure from the layers above, making it look like frozen time capsules. “Thudd!!!” We all turned to see what had fallen—Farini’s phone. She had been taking pictures when it slipped from her hands and crashed onto the ice. She quickly picked it up, checked the damage, and let out a sigh of relief. “Thanks to the tempered glass,” my inner me said, glad that at least the screen was saved. After that minor panic attack, she shook it off and went back to enjoying the hike like a champ. On our way back, we took a less-travelled path, carving our way through the ice with our crampons. But no matter how exhilarating it was, it was freezing. Our body warmers barely kept us from turning into icicles, but damn, was it worth it. “Yes, thank me,” Farini smirked, reminding us that it was her idea. 
 “Okay, fineeeee,” I replied, as mockingly as possible. By 2 PM, we were back at the pickup point, ready for our next adventure—Diamond Beach. Diamond Beach - Where Ice Meets the Ocean Another day, another breathtaking drive.

The entire road was flanked by glaciers, and with the sun setting behind us, the sky transformed into a canvas of deep oranges and purples. It was the kind of view you remember for a lifetime.
 By 3:30 PM, we reached Diamond Beach—and let me tell you, the tiredness vanished instantly. 
 Imagine this: huge ice blocks, crystal clear, scattered across black volcanic sand, with waves crashing and dragging pieces back into the sea.  It  was beyond mesmerising. 
 We spent the next hour walking along the shore, clicking pictures, and soaking in the moment as the sun dipped below the horizon. Northern Lights & Parking Disaster Back at our cabin, just 2 km away, I turned to Rinku—  “Macha, we have to hunt for Northern Lights tonight.” We hadn’t spotted them yet, and Iceland isn’t the best place for auroras—Finland and Norway are closer to the North Pole and get much stronger displays. Plus, December isn’t the peak time here. As we reached our stay, Rinku took a wrong left and parked behind  the house instead of the usual parking spot. Both me and Farini made him turn back and park correctly. “What idiots you both are! I had parked ahead for a reason!” Rinku growled. Turns out, the actual parking spot was covered in frozen ice, making it harder to unload the luggage. Rinku, being smarter than us for once, had parked where it was easier to get down. Too late. We were stuck now. Every Day is a Beer Day We settled in, discussing whether we should do another Crystal Ice Cave tour. The lady bosses (read: the wives) gave their approvals, and without wasting time, we booked our tickets with Arctic Adventures. As we relaxed, Rinku kept peeking outside the window, checking for any trace of the Northern Lights. I quickly opened the Hello Aurora app to check the probability. Suited in thermal layers, we drove to the Glacier Lagoon parking lot—a perfect dark spot for aurora hunting. At first, nothing. But as we clicked pictures to test for light traces —yes, there it was. Slowly, the aurora intensified, spreading across the sky in an oval shape before dancing lightly. It wasn’t the craziest  display as we expected, but it was absolutely worth it. After an hour of freezing our asses off, we drove back to our cabin, grabbed our blankets, and called it a night. 07/12/2024 - Ice Caves, Freezing Lagoons & A Booking Blunder Another day, another adventure—but this time, without  an intense hike. Or so we thought. We arrived at Diamond Beach parking and had a sudden realization—parking fees in Iceland aren’t optional. Up until the previous day, we had assumed it was voluntary since no one ever checked. Turns out, if you miss paying, you get charged 4X the original amount. Classic tourist trap Luckily, we had paid at most places, but a few may have slipped. Not willing to take any chances, I quickly opened my Parka app and grabbed a one-day ticket. With that sorted, we hopped into the Super Jeeps, ready to hit the icy roads toward another round of glacier exploration. 
 The Blue Ice Cave - A Natural Wonder The ride to the base site took around 30 minutes, and from there, we geared up for yet another glacier hike. This time, we were on the other side of the massive Vatnajökull Glacier, and it was even bigger than the one we explored the previous day. Following the crampon trails left by other hikers, we started trekking, with icy winds trying to knock us over. Thankfully, the path had support ropes, and we all made it safely to the entrance of the Blue Ice Cave. And damn—this cave was massive. Our guide explained how these natural ice caves form and how deep they can go. We switched on our head torches and started walking inside. The moment the light hit the frozen walls, the reflections bouncing off the deep blue ice were nothing short of magical. After soaking in the beauty and clicking our mandatory pictures, we moved on to the next cave—whose name I’d already forgotten. 😛 This second cave was smaller, but transparent rather than blue, giving it a crystal-like appearance. Not as grand as the first one, but still very  cool. By the time we returned to the base, it was past noon, and we realized we hadn’t actually seen Glacier Lagoon up close. So, we made a quick stop there—though with Iceland’s temperatures, “chilling” at the lagoon took on a very literal  meaning. 😛 A Traffic Nightmare & The Silfra Booking Blunder Our next stop? Minniborgir Cottages, our stay for the night. We had plans for Silfra Snorkeling the next day, but here’s the problem—we hadn’t booked it yet. No big deal, we thought. We’d sort it out once we reached the stay. But Iceland had other plans. Barely an hour into our drive, we hit a massive traffic jam.  Not just slow-moving—completely stuck . For the next 2.5 hours, we sat at the same spot, not moving an inch. Imagine the frustration.  At  this point, we were already running way behind schedule. In the chaos, Cutti and Farini started checking out Silfra diving pictures, and I asked for confirmation to book it. Without reading much of the details, I booked it immediately. Big mistake. By the time we finally reached our cabin, it was past 11:30 PM. Exhausted, we had a quick dinner and crashed, knowing we had to leave by 9 AM sharp the next day. But little did we know… A surprise was waiting for us. 08/12/2024 - The Day Iceland Taught us a Lesson I stretched my body, waking up in disguise, more like denial. I wasn’t in the mood to move. After days of non-stop adventure, my body was begging for a chill day. But we had one last activity, Snorkeling in Silfra. Silfra Fissure  is a glacier meltwater-filled rift formed by the drift of the Eurasian and North American tectonic plates. It’s one of a kind—there’s nowhere else in the world where you can swim between two continents. So, despite my reluctance, we mentally prepared ourselves and hurried to leave on time… yet failed.  It  was already 9:20 AM by the time we hit the road. To make things worse, it had snowed heavily overnight. The thin layer of ice on the roads meant we couldn’t drive fast either. Great. Lesson - Time Waits for No One & Read the Fine Print Fifteen minutes away from the site, my phone rang—it was the guide. I assured him we’d be there in 10-15 minutes, but his response? “If you’re late, you’ll have to miss it.” I thought he was just trying to scare us, but nope—he meant it. As soon as we arrived, Rinku told us to go check in while he parked the car. But the moment we reached the guide— “You’re late. We cannot take you.” No amount of pleading, bargaining, or puppy eyes worked. He stood his ground. Þingvellir National Park issues strict slots for different travel agencies, and they are not flexible. We had missed our window, and there was nothing we could do. The guide suggested calling customer support to check for another slot in the afternoon, so we clung to that tiny shred of hope. As we called Arctic Adventures, another surprise hit us—swimming was mandatory. I had been under the illusion that we’d get life jackets, but no—we’d be in wetsuits. Technically, you won’t drown, but it didn’t matter. Farini wasn’t okay with it.  Neither was Cutti since she wasn’t a confident swimmer in flowing water. But even if we were ready, luck wasn’t on our side. Arctic Adventures denied our request for another slot. No refund, no rescheduling—just money down the drain. 
 Frustrated, I later checked the booking confirmation—and there it was, in bold, highlighted letters: "Participants must arrive at least 15 minutes before the activity start time." Of course, we hadn’t read it. And just like that, we paid the price for our ignorance. The importance of reaching on time was a harsh but valuable lesson we learned that day. The Silfra Fissure Since we were already there, we took a small stroll near the pond, soaking in the breathtaking view of the tectonic plates from outside .  By  then, it had started snowing, and we got another yellow alert—not the best weather to stick around. So, we started heading back to Reykjavik. On the way, Farini finally snapped—“At least today we’ll eat outside! I’m tired of ready-made food.” Fair enough. After days of surviving on packed meals, we decided to treat ourselves. We checked into yet another cozy Airbnb and headed straight to Domino’s. And guess what? Two fully loaded pizzas cost us 8,000 INR. Absolutely insane—but totally deserved. 😛 For the first time in days, we did absolutely nothing. No hikes. No rushing. No itinerary. Just chilling, chatting, and soaking in the local vibes. And honestly? It was much needed. As we sat there, unwinding from the chaos of the day, Cutti suddenly turned to me—“Mattu, what about whale watching? When are we going?” If Ice Caves and Glacier Hikes were mine and Rinku’s  must-do activities, then Whale watching was Cutti’s  ultimate bucket list item. With a smirk, I looked at her. “Guess we have another adventure left.” 09/12/2024 - The Whale Watching Day It was the  much-awaited day for my wife—her eyes sparkled with excitement from the moment she woke up. 
 We had booked our cruise with Blue Iceland, and honestly, the whole experience was worth every krona we spent. Having been haunted by the ghost of our missed snorkelling slot, we left no room for error this time. We made sure to be on time—no detours, no last-minute coffee cravings, no nothing. Just focused commitment to whales, haha Once we boarded the massive cruise ship, we grabbed a good spot on the deck, layered up like onions, and braced ourselves for the cold breeze. The sea was calm, the air crisp, and the sky painted in that dull Icelandic gray that somehow makes everything look more dramatic. After about 30 minutes into the ride, the crew pointed at something near the horizon—and suddenly, a massive whale surfaced just a few meters away. The first glimpse was unreal. A splash and a tail flip, it felt like time paused for a second. There were gasps and cheers all around, but for a moment, we just stood there silently, soaking it all in. Then, as if trying to beat its own performance, another whale popped up on the other side. I swear, it was like they were having a family gathering and we were uninvited guests who got lucky.  For the next hour, we were treated to multiple sightings After the cruise docked, we were cold, a little wet from the sea mist, but fully satisfied. We headed to our go-to comfort zone—Domino’s (our unofficial trip sponsor at this point)—grabbed some snacks, warmed our hands on the pizza boxes, and laughed through the day’s memories. Wrapped in layers and smiles, we called it a night, hearts full and bucket lists shorter by one unforgettable experience. 10/12/2024 - The Lagoon The next day was our visit to the iconic Blue Lagoon—the grand finale of our Icelandic saga. To be honest, we were a bit sceptical about it. Some folks had told us it’s overpriced, overrated, and basically a glorified hot tub. But let me tell you, it’s absolutely one-of-a-kind. Keeping the cost aside for a moment (which, yes, is expensive), the Blue Lagoon stands apart from every other lagoon in Iceland. While the rest are more like typical hot spring lagoons, this one is uniquely silica-based, giving it that dreamy blue hue and those skincare-promising, Instagram-worthy vibes. And let's not forget the free drink you get right in the pool. Beer, wine, smoothies—whatever floats your tired traveller soul. Imagine lounging in warm, mineral-rich water, a drink in one hand, face slathered with a white silica mask, and the cold wind just barely kissing your forehead. That kind of convenience and indulgence? Totally worth it. We spent a good few hours marinating in the pool, pretending we were in a skincare ad, while also clicking the most unhinged, scary-looking pictures imaginable. I finally got a picture with Rinku where both of us looked like zombie snowmen with spa aspirations. A personal win. But all that bliss came with a small side effect—silica dehydration is real, folks. I started feeling dizzy out of nowhere like I had just walked through a desert in thermal swimwear. Thankfully, I had known beforehand that it’s best to step out the moment dehydration hits. So, I somehow dragged myself out, hardly could take the full shower, grabbed a snack and chugged water like my life depended on it—because honestly, it kind of did at that point. The Blue Lagoon I’d say Blue Lagoon was the perfect way to end the trip . A spa-like, peaceful, floaty feeling after days of hiking, freezing, and missing activities. It truly felt like the calm after the chaos. We packed our bags with heavy hearts, as it was our last night in Iceland. The trip was coming to an end, but the memories? Oh, they were just getting warmed up. 11/12/2024 - Final Flickers of Fire & Farewell  Time to wrap up the Iceland trip, and like every good ending, it came with a touch of nostalgia and a whole lot of last-minute scrambling. 
 We quickly fixed ourselves a breakfast and headed out for some final souvenir hunting. Our first stop? The famous Hallgrímskirkja church. We clicked a few quick photos, grabbed some souvenirs, and took a relaxed stroll through the nearby streets soaking in Reykjavik’s charm one last time. Then came the unexpected highlight: The Lava Show—Harini’s much-needed bucket list experience. Honestly, when I first heard about it, I rolled my eyes a bit thinking, “It’s molten lava in a man-made setup, how exciting could it be?” But oh, how wrong I was. The show turned out to be super insightful and thrilling. You actually witness real lava flowing—yes, REAL. FLAMING. LAVA, right in front of you, melting rocks, forming silica. It was not just a visual treat but also a genuinely educational experience. Nature's fury, but in a safe, tourist-friendly setting. The final picture We even got a chunk of cooled lava stone as a souvenir. Like, how often do you take a literal piece of Icelandic fire home with you? And just like that, with a hot stone in our bags and memories hotter than the lava itself, we made our way to the airport, boarded our flight to Venice, and said our final goodbyes to the land of ice and fire. And that’s a wrap on Iceland. 10/10. Would freeze, hike, fall, drink, and almost miss activities all over again. Chasing wonders in Iceland! textData.text: "Rinku, what about our Iceland trip?" I questioned, sipping on Old Monk during a laid-back weekend getaway near Chikmagalur.

Rinku, deep in thought, replied, “Not sure… I’m planning a career switch. If things settle down by December, maybe we can go in late January for yours and Harini’s birthday—or the first week of February.”
I wasn’t entirely convinced. With 14 leaves about to lapse, I was eager to make it happen this year itself. If we postponed now, it would be the second time. This trip
had
to happen this year. Luck, however, had other plans. Rinku secured a fantastic job, and just like that, we were set to hit the Icy road for Iceland!
01/12/2024 - The Journey Begins
As expected, the drama began early. At Frankfurt, Germany, we were denied boarding for our connecting flight to Reykjavik—
despite
being at the gate on time. The delay from our Bangalore-to-Frankfurt flight had caused chaos, and to make things worse, Lufthansa overbooked the flight.

Their customer service? Absolutely pathetic. Four hours of standing in a never-moving queue for rebooking, without so much as a courtesy call to inform us or offer an alternative. Classic Lufthansa, right?

Eventually, after what felt like an eternity, we got rebooked—via Sweden—to Reykjavik. By the time we arrived at Reykjavik Airport, it was close to midnight. Exhausted and freezing, we discovered that our self-drive rental had been
cancelled
due to the late arrival.
After some scrambling, we managed to strike a direct deal with the same provider. Same cost, but 50 euros extra for late-night pickup. Considering the circumstances, we took it.
“Looks pretty neat,” I mumbled through chattering teeth, taking a quick look at our Vitara Brezza in the dim airport light.
The car seemed ready for the adventure ahead—if only we were too. We drove straight to our Airbnb and collapsed into bed, knowing we had a couple of hours of driving to do the next morning.
02/12/2024 - A Windy Affair with Snæfellsnes
I woke up thinking it was too early—the sky was still blanketed in darkness. Just as I started to roll over,
Rinku’s voice, “Macha, we’re late for breakfast. Let’s go!”.
It was 8:30 AM, and I hadn’t even realized it. Iceland’s winter darkness had already messed with my sense of time.

We quickly freshened up, excitement bubbling as the thought of starting our road trip sank in. However with a slight doubt —could we make it through Snæfellsnes before the yellow weather alerts kicked in post-lunch?
After savouring our complimentary English breakfast, we loaded the car and hit the road towards the Snæfellsnes Peninsula. We were en route to our first destination—
Ytri Tunga Beach
—to spot some seals.
Seals, Wind, and (Mild) Chaos
“It’s too cold to even step out!”
the girls complained as they opened the car doors, bracing against the biting winter wind.
Well, it was Iceland in December—what else could we expect?
We started walking towards the beach, reading the signboards that reminded us to keep a respectful distance from the shore and to stay quiet to avoid disturbing the seals.
“Look at that shoal of seals!”, suddenly, someone pointed.
We turned to see a group of seals swimming about 300 meters away. Though our lenses couldn’t capture much, our eyes did, and it was a memory worth keeping.
Further along the shore, a lone seal was sprawled lazily on a rock, upside down.
“That seal reminded me of my wife!” 😂
The Overrated (but Beautiful) Black Church
Our next stop was the
Black Church at Búðir
. A stark contrast of black against white snowy landscapes, the church is small but undeniably charming. While it lacks the grandeur of European cathedrals, its uniqueness lies in its simplicity.
“Do you know why it’s black?” I asked.
“Black absorbs everything, right? Isn’t that counterproductive in the cold?
”Rinku shrugged.
“No idea. Let’s move before we freeze.
By 2 PM, the girls declared it was lunchtime. Unfortunately, we hadn’t packed lunch due to the previous day’s flight delays, so we decided to grab something en route.
Finding a restaurant in Iceland during winter feels like finding logic in my friend group—rare and improbable. But we managed to spot one, thanks to a helpful signboard directing us to take a detour.
“I’ll have to sell my kidney to finish this trip,” I exclaimed, staring at the prices. A burger and two mini fries set us back a whopping 5,200 ISK.
Yes, Iceland is expensive—everything is imported—but the quality and hygiene are top-notch.
Battling the Yellow Alert
“Macha, the yellow alert has started. Should we keep driving?” Rinku asked, concerned.
“No way we’re turning back,” I replied, firm but slightly sceptical.
We had never experienced Iceland’s infamous storms, and I wasn’t sure how bad it could get.
After checking alternate routes, we found one road already closed due to winds. The other two were passable—one longer and one shorter.
Our planned route was the longer one, as we had hoped to catch the sunset at
Djúpalónssandur
, the Black Sand Beach.
In Iceland, sunsets are a rarity, as the skies are often overcast. Still, we decided to risk it. Iceland’s winters are bearable, but the winds are what make it brutal.

By the time we reached Djúpalónssandur, the winds were no joke. As I stretched to wear my jacket, the gusts pushed me backwards, jacket and all. Iceland’s winds are a force to be reckoned with—more chilling than the winter cold itself.
We couldn’t get past the parking area, but that didn’t stop Rinku, Cutti, and me from having fun. We jumped and played, letting the winds toss us around like kids rediscovering their innocence.
“You guys are such kids,” muttered Farini, shivering as she slammed the car door shut.
The Yellow Alert - Strong winds by picking up the ice
After braving the winds, we made it to our cozy B&B for the night. It was warm, welcoming, and exactly what we needed. We prepared tasty biryani and wrapped our day.
Snæfellsnes had given us its best—and its worst—but it was all part of the adventure we’d come for.
3/12/2024 - Kirkjufell, Lava Falls & A Love Book Surprise
Our third day in Iceland, and the excitement still hadn’t faded. We were finally going to visit
Kirkjufell
, the iconic cone-shaped mountain that seemed to be plastered across every Iceland travel blog.
“I still don’t get why this is so hyped,” I muttered to myself while scrolling through yet another blog post about it.
Maybe it was the shape, maybe the surrounding landscape.
From our Airbnb’s living room, the view was spectacular. Kirkjufell stood majestically, framed by the crisp winter air and the first light of the day. It was
that
close.
While breakfast was being prepared, I grabbed a coffee and flipped through the magazines stacked on the table. One book caught my attention—
“Love.”
Curious, I randomly opened a page. My eyes opened wide. Right there, a couple was in an intimate position—Missionary.
I turned the page. Next up—Cowgirl.
“Wait, what kind of book is this?!”
Excited, I called my wife and friends over.
“You pervert!” Farini snapped, walking away.
I turned another page, expecting more… but what I saw next threw me off completely—a toddler playing with a dog. The next page? A rustic mother and son standing in a farm field.
“Oh damn… This book isn’t about
that
kind of love… It’s about
all
forms of love.”
I stared at it for a second, processing my newfound enlightenment. I turned to Cutti and the others.
“Wow. Happy realisation,” my wife said.
Farini, still unimpressed, threw in some sarcasm.
And with that, we packed our bags, spun the wheel, and set off towards
Kirkjufell
Kirkjufell & The Drive to Hraunfossar
As expected, it was freezing outside, but the view made up for it. Kirkjufell stood tall, its conical peak contrasting beautifully against the sky, with
Kirkjufellsfoss
flowing gracefully opposite to it.
Happy us @ Kirkjufell
For context—foss means waterfall in Icelandic. This one? Small, cute… kinda like my wife. 😛
After soaking in the view, we continued towards
Hraunfossar
, also known as
Lava Falls
. The drive itself was breathtaking—everywhere we looked, the landscape screamed
wow, wow, and wow.

We finally reached the falls, and let me tell you—this was something else. The waterfalls stretched across hundreds of meters, with ice creeping in from the edges but not fully freezing over. Water still trickled through various channels, creating a mesmerizing effect.

textData.text: A kind lady who offered to take our pictures casually explained, “This waterfall formed when lava caves collapsed after an eruption long ago.”
I nodded, pretending I knew
exactly
when that happened. 😛
By the time we checked the clock, it was already 4 PM—and we still hadn’t eaten. Starving, we hurried back to the car park to dig into our
very
frozen packed lunch.
Thankfully, we had hot chocolate to go with it, because the café had a
buy something or no washroom
policy.
Fun fact: Most public washrooms in Iceland are free, but some places make you purchase something before you can access them. Rare, but it happens.
With daylight gone, we started our drive back to Reykjavik, passing through the
Hvalfjörður Tunnel
—an absolute monster at
5,800 meters
“This is ducking long,” I muttered, genuinely impressed.
After reaching Reykjavik, we checked into
Dalur - Hi Eco Hostel
This place was awesome, keypad-secured doors for both the hostel entrance and the rooms, all automated.
No human interaction—just an email with our booking details and PIN codes.
Efficient, yet slightly annoying in case if we need something.
The kitchen? A dream. Every appliance you could ask for, ready to go.
We ended the night with a
true
comfort meal—
Plain white rice, Steaming hot rasam, Chutney pudi, and Beer.
Oh, and of course, curd—because what kind of South Indian would I be without it?
We installed
Hello Aurora

, an aurora spotting app, which provides real-time updates on aurora activity levels and visibility. Although there wasn’t much activity forecasted for that night, we decided to give it one last hopeful try. We drove to the edge of Reykjavik, to the
Grotta Island Lighthouse
, a popular northern lights viewing spot. As we reached, the temperature plummeted and it was
biting
cold.

Despite shivering and hopping in and out of the car like confused penguins, we waited patiently, eyes scanning the horizon. An hour passed… and nothing. No sign of the lights, no colours in the sky—just the howling wind and the freezing air. Finally, we gave up and decided to head back to the hostel to sleep.
And just like that, another day in Iceland came to a close.
04/12/2024 - The Land of Ice, Fire & Cutti’s Ice-Skating Stunt
The morning was chilled, quite literally, but there wasn’t much rush to start our day. Still, we had to move quickly—daylight in Iceland is as rare as a budget-friendly meal here.
After a quick breakfast at the hostel, we packed up and checked out, making our way to
Bónus
, the go-to supermarket in Reykjavik. This was our last stop in the city for the next four days, so we had to stock up on essentials.

Supermarkets in Reykjavik? Cheap and convenient.
Supermarkets in other parts of Iceland? Uncommon. 
Also, most shut early in the evening.
We grabbed everything we could—fruits, berries, cookies, chocolates—and hit the road towards our next stop:
Geysir.
Ever since I saw a video of a geyser erupting on a fellow traveller’s phone back at our Airbnb, I had been buzzing with excitement. Seeing it in real life? That was a whole other level.
As we parked and walked towards the geothermal area, we could literally
feel
the heat beneath our feet. The contrast was insane—freezing cold air, yet steaming ground.
Along the path, we passed small boiling ponds, their surfaces bubbling aggressively like a giant’s cauldron.
“Good thing there’s a caution board,” my brain noted, silently appreciating that Iceland doesn’t believe in natural selection.
Finally, we reached the
Great Geysir.
The pool itself wasn’t huge—about the size of a traditional well—but the anticipation was real. The water boiled continuously, simmering for a few minutes before…
BOOM!

A massive jet of scalding water shot 10-15 feet into the air, creating a surreal spectacle. The cycle is repeated every few minutes—boil, build-up, explosion, cooldown, repeat. An absolute marvel of nature.
The Geysir
Iceland truly lives up to its title—the land of ice and fire.
To warm ourselves up, we grabbed some hot chocolate from a restaurant near the parking lot—a small but delicious bonus.
Gullfoss - The Golden Falls & Cutti’s Slip of Fate
Next up—
Gullfoss
, aka the
Golden Falls
. Some legends say Vikings threw gold into the waters, giving it its name. I say it’s just an
expensive
looking waterfall.

The moment we stepped out of the car, Cutti’s words summed up the situation perfectly—“Ah, it’s so freezing cold,” she stammered, struggling to walk as sudden gusts of wind made the already chilling temperatures even worse.
As I stood there, soaking in the beauty, I suddenly heard—
Thuddddd!
I turned around to see Cutti lying flat on the ice, looking
very
betrayed by the ground.
Damn my thoughts—I was just admiring the beauty of the place, and the universe immediately struck her with
Nazar.
Luckily, aside from a bruised right hand, she was fine.
Off to Flúðir - The Coziest Wrap to the Day
Instead of driving back to Reykjavik to start our journey towards
Jökulsárlón
, we took a more direct route and booked a private
cabin in Flúðir
for the night.
And wow—what a place. Cozy wooden interiors, a huge TV, and a perfect setting to wind down.
We cooked some noodles, cracked open some beers, and tuned into Netflix.
The movie of the night? "Lucky Bhaskar"—because nothing says adventure like a Telugu movie in the middle of Iceland.
The Mild Aurora - View from our Airbnb

textData.text: And just like that, another epic day came to an end.
05/12/2024 - A Day of Frozen Falls & Nearly Getting Blown Away
The previous night, we discovered that
Sky Lagoon
was just a mile away from our stay.
“Of course, why would we miss dipping ourselves in a thermal pool?” Rinku declared, making it clear that this would be the first thing we did today.

Waking up early in Iceland is a challenge—especially when the bed is warm, and the outside world is freezing. But by 7 AM, we were up, prepping breakfast and packing lunch to ensure we made it to the lagoon early, avoiding the crowds.
Luckily, when we reached, the place was
almost
empty—just around ten people in the entire pool. We quickly changed into our swimwear and took a dip.
“Ooohhhh it’s cold!” the girls shrieked as they ran through the icy air toward the pool. But the moment we got in, the magic of Iceland’s geothermal waters took over.
Sky lagoon

Thermal pools are one of Iceland’s biggest treasures. Sky Lagoon is no exception—a huge 100x100 pond filled with natural hot water drawn from underground. Since the water at the source is around 100 degrees Celsius, it’s mixed with cold water before being routed to the pool, making it just
perfect
for soaking in.
Smiles after a steamy hot bath amidst of teeth-biting cold

textData.text: After a blissful dip, we grabbed some breakfast and hit the road towards the waterfalls of the day.
Seljalandsfoss & Gljúfrabúi - The Frozen Beauties
Today was all about
frozen waterfalls
—and the first on our list was
Seljalandsfoss
, a towering cascade that crashes down from over 100 feet. You can feel the mist on your face
even from a distance
As we admired the fall, Farini suddenly shoved her phone in my face.
“Balu, look at this! It’s amazing! Why aren’t we going here?”
she demanded, showing me an Instagram reel of another stunning waterfall.
I sighed. This is why people should check the itinerary.
“Huh, that’s literally our next stop—
Gljúfrabúi
,” I replied, dripping with sarcasm.
“Okay fineeee,” she muttered in her classic mocking tone.
Gljúfrabúi
is lesser-known but equally breathtaking—a partially frozen waterfall hidden inside a narrow canyon.
What we
didn’t
know? It was just a short walk from Seljalandsfoss.
Instead of walking, we blindly followed Google Maps… which led us straight to a private property with a huge “NO ENTRY” sign.
“Nice. Now what?” Rinku sighed.
We turned back, defeated, only to spot people walking towards the falls.
“There, there! People are walking!” I pointed excitedly.

Rinku quickly parked, and we joined the group. As we stepped onto the narrow, icy path, the sheer beauty of Gljúfrabúi hit us. The falls were hidden behind a rocky entrance, making the experience even more surreal.
The only downside? The path was super slippery, and at some points, we had to step into freezing water.
Rinku, being the genius that he is, had forgotten his gloves. Holding onto the icy boulders for balance? Not fun. Within minutes, his hands turned numb, forcing him to run back

textData.text: Skógafoss - The Grand Finale of Waterfalls
After our icy adventure, we continued towards
Vik
, where we had booked our next stay. But before that, one last stop—
Skógafoss
And let me just say—this waterfall is 100/10.
It’s similar in height to Seljalandsfoss, but way wider, making it even more dramatic. The best part? The partially frozen ice leading up to it, where you could
literally
see water flowing beneath the fresh ice sheet.
I now understood the quote “the journey is more beautiful than the destination.”
Of course, we had to trouble a photographer nearby to get some decent pictures.
“Macha, let’s move. It’s already past sunset,” Rinku reminded us, snapping us out of our waterfall trance.
We had 90 minutes to reach our Airbnb and started driving towards Vik.
The Airbnb Disaster & The Night We Almost Got Blown Away
After a long drive, we finally arrived at
Kirkjubæjarklaustur
, a small village between Vik and Hofn.
“Where’s our stay?” Rinku asked, frowning at the lack of, well… anything.
“I don’t know. This is where the Airbnb location ended,” I replied, equally confused.
I opened the Airbnb to read this message from the host
“Please don’t follow the Airbnb location. Our actual place is 30 km away. Here’s the real landmark.”

30. Freaking. Kilometers. Behind.
I was pissed. Who even uploads the wrong location on Airbnb?! What an ass!
As we sat there fuming, the winds suddenly picked up. Hard. The car started shaking violently. Yellow alert.
For a moment, I genuinely wondered if we’d get
blown away
. Luckily, we had four heavy asses inside and a trunk full of luggage anchoring us down. 😂
At this point, I wasn’t in the mood to drive back. I called Airbnb, got the booking cancelled, and they suggested a new stay—
Bikers Farm Iceland.
In my frustration, I booked it without reading the description. Bad move.
As we reached, the winds had only gotten worse—Rinku, carrying three bags, nearly got blown off his feet. That’s how strong it was.

Then came another surprise—the kitchen and bathrooms were separate from the rooms, meaning we had to walk 50 meters through deadly winds just to pee, and to make things worse, the heater was small, barely functional for Iceland’s brutal cold.
At this point, we were too tired and somehow managed to sleep through the chaos.
The only best part of the day? A good tummy full of spicy noodles and a beer.
Also, nobody woke me and Rinku up for a bathroom run.
And with that, another legendary day in Iceland came to a close.
06/12/2024 - Walking on Ice, Chasing Lights & Parking Disaster
This was it—the day we had been waiting for. The
Skaftafell Ice Cave & Glacier Hike
was finally happening.
We reached Arctic Adventures at 9:10 AM, a good ten minutes late. Typical. If there’s one thing we Indians need to work on, it’s arriving
on time

. We were the last ones to reach, but thankfully, the guides were still helping others gear up. We quickly filled out safety forms, strapped on our helmets, and grabbed our ice axes—because, of course, what’s a glacier hike without feeling like a Viking?
A van took us to the starting point of the
Vatnajökull Glacier
, the largest in Iceland, covering
15% of the country
. Yeah, it’s
that
massive.
The Glacier That Wasn’t Black—It Was Just Covered in Sand
After a short walk, we stopped to put on our crampons, and the real hike began.
At first, the trail looked completely black, and we assumed we’d see the glacier after this stretch. But nope—the trail itself was a glacier, just covered in black volcanic ash.
As we walked, our crampons scraped the surface, revealing the pure ice underneath.
d
Walking on a glacier—wowww. One of the coolest (literally) things I’ve done.
Then, up ahead, we saw it—a massive, crystal-clear glacier wall, stretching so high it seemed to touch the sky, like an ocean frozen in time.
The sun was just rising over the horizon, casting a golden glow over the icy landscape. The sky turned into a breathtaking mix of orange and blue hues, making the whole experience
unreal

textData.text: After a solid trek, we finally reached the
Blue Ice Cave

The cave is semi-natural—guides check it daily and carve a path if needed since glaciers constantly move, albeit at a tortoise’s pace. The entrance was a narrow passage, allowing only one person at a time. Walking inside was surreal—the ice had trapped bubbles due to pressure from the layers above, making it look like frozen time capsules.
“Thudd!!!”
We all turned to see what had fallen—Farini’s phone.
She had been taking pictures when it slipped from her hands and crashed onto the ice. She quickly picked it up, checked the damage, and let out a sigh of relief.
“Thanks to the tempered glass,” my inner me said, glad that at least the screen was saved.
After that minor panic attack, she shook it off and went back to enjoying the hike like a champ.

On our way back, we took a less-travelled path, carving our way through the ice with our crampons. But no matter how exhilarating it was, it was freezing. Our body warmers barely kept us from turning into icicles, but damn, was it worth it.
“Yes, thank me,” Farini smirked, reminding us that it was her idea.
“Okay, fineeeee,” I replied, as mockingly as possible.
By 2 PM, we were back at the pickup point, ready for our next adventure—Diamond Beach.
Diamond Beach - Where Ice Meets the Ocean

Another day, another breathtaking drive.

The entire road was flanked by glaciers, and with the sun setting behind us, the sky transformed into a canvas of deep oranges and purples. It was the kind of view you remember for a lifetime.
By 3:30 PM, we reached Diamond Beach—and let me tell you, the tiredness vanished instantly.
Imagine this: huge ice blocks, crystal clear, scattered across black volcanic sand, with waves crashing and dragging pieces back into the
sea.
It
was beyond mesmerising.

textData.text: We spent the next hour walking along the shore, clicking pictures, and soaking in the
moment as the sun dipped below the horizon.
Northern Lights & Parking Disaster
Back at our cabin, just 2 km away, I turned to Rinku—
“Macha, we have to hunt for Northern Lights tonight.”
We hadn’t spotted them yet, and Iceland isn’t the best place for auroras—Finland and Norway are closer to the North Pole and get much stronger displays. Plus, December isn’t the peak time here.
As we reached our stay, Rinku took a wrong left and parked
behind
the house instead of the usual parking spot. Both me and Farini made him turn back and park correctly.
“What idiots you both are! I had parked ahead for a reason!” Rinku growled.
Turns out, the actual parking spot was covered in frozen ice, making it harder to unload the luggage. Rinku, being smarter than us for once, had parked where it was easier to get down.
Too late. We were stuck now.
Every Day is a Beer Day

We settled in, discussing whether we should do another Crystal Ice Cave tour. The lady bosses (read: the wives) gave their approvals, and without wasting time, we booked our tickets with Arctic Adventures.
As we relaxed, Rinku kept peeking outside the window, checking for any trace of the Northern Lights. I quickly opened the Hello Aurora app to check the probability.
Suited in thermal layers, we drove to the Glacier Lagoon parking lot—a perfect dark spot for aurora hunting.
At first, nothing. But as we clicked pictures to test for
light traces
—yes, there it was.
Slowly, the aurora intensified, spreading across the sky in an oval shape before dancing lightly.
It wasn’t the
craziest
display as we expected, but it was absolutely worth it.
After an hour of freezing our asses off, we drove back to our cabin, grabbed our blankets, and called it a night.
07/12/2024 - Ice Caves, Freezing Lagoons & A Booking Blunder
Another day, another adventure—but this time,
without
an intense hike. Or so we thought.

We arrived at Diamond Beach parking and had a sudden realization—parking fees in Iceland aren’t optional. Up until the previous day, we had assumed it was voluntary since no one ever checked. Turns out, if you miss paying, you get charged 4X the original amount. Classic tourist trap
Luckily, we had paid at most places, but a few may have slipped. Not willing to take any chances, I quickly opened my Parka app and grabbed a one-day ticket.
With that sorted, we hopped into the Super Jeeps, ready to hit the icy roads toward another round of glacier exploration.
The Blue Ice Cave - A Natural Wonder

The ride to the base site took around 30 minutes, and from there, we geared up for yet another glacier hike. This time, we were on the other side of the massive Vatnajökull Glacier, and it was even bigger than the one we explored the previous day.

Following the crampon trails left by other hikers, we started trekking, with icy winds trying to knock us over. Thankfully, the path had support ropes, and we all made it safely to the entrance of the Blue Ice Cave.
And damn—this cave was massive.
Our guide explained how these natural ice caves form and how deep they can go. We switched on our head torches and started walking inside.

The moment the light hit the frozen walls, the reflections bouncing off the deep blue ice were nothing short of magical. After soaking in the beauty and clicking our mandatory pictures, we moved on to the next cave—whose name I’d already forgotten. 😛
This second cave was smaller, but transparent rather than blue, giving it a crystal-like appearance. Not as grand as the first one, but still
very
cool.

By the time we returned to the base, it was past noon, and we realized we hadn’t actually seen Glacier Lagoon up close. So, we made a quick stop there—though with Iceland’s temperatures, “chilling” at the lagoon took on a very
literal
meaning. 😛
A Traffic Nightmare & The Silfra Booking Blunder
Our next stop? Minniborgir Cottages, our stay for the night.
We had plans for Silfra Snorkeling the next day, but here’s the problem—we hadn’t booked it yet. No big deal, we thought. We’d sort it out once we reached the stay.
But Iceland had other plans.
Barely an hour into our drive, we hit a massive traffic jam.
Not just slow-moving—completely stuck
. For the next 2.5 hours, we sat at the same spot, not moving an inch. Imagine the
frustration.
At
this point, we were already running way behind schedule. In the chaos, Cutti and Farini started checking out Silfra diving pictures, and I asked for confirmation to book it.
Without reading much of the details, I booked it immediately.
Big mistake.
By the time we finally reached our cabin, it was past 11:30 PM. Exhausted, we had a quick dinner and crashed, knowing we had to leave by 9 AM sharp the next day.
But little did we know…
A surprise was waiting for us.
08/12/2024 - The Day Iceland Taught us a Lesson

I stretched my body, waking up in disguise, more like denial. I wasn’t in the mood to move. After days of non-stop adventure, my body was begging for a chill day. But we had one last activity, Snorkeling in Silfra.
Silfra Fissure

is a glacier meltwater-filled rift formed by the drift of the Eurasian and North American tectonic plates. It’s one of a kind—there’s nowhere else in the world where you can swim between two continents.
So, despite my reluctance, we mentally prepared ourselves and hurried to leave on time… yet
failed.
It
was already 9:20 AM by the time we hit the road.
To make things worse, it had snowed heavily overnight. The thin layer of ice on the roads meant we couldn’t drive fast either. Great.
Lesson - Time Waits for No One & Read the Fine Print
Fifteen minutes away from the site, my phone rang—it was the guide.
I assured him we’d be there in 10-15 minutes, but his response? “If you’re late, you’ll have to miss it.”
I thought he was just trying to scare us, but nope—he meant it.
As soon as we arrived, Rinku told us to go check in while he parked the car. But the moment we reached the guide—
“You’re late. We cannot take you.”
No amount of pleading, bargaining, or puppy eyes worked. He stood his ground.
Þingvellir National Park issues strict slots for different travel agencies, and they are not flexible.
We had missed our window, and there was nothing we could do.
The guide suggested calling customer support to check for another slot in the afternoon, so we clung to that tiny shred of hope.
As we called Arctic Adventures, another surprise hit us—swimming was mandatory. I had been under the illusion that we’d get life jackets, but no—we’d be in wetsuits.
Technically, you won’t drown, but it didn’t matter. Farini wasn’t okay with it.  Neither was Cutti since she wasn’t a confident swimmer in flowing water.
But even if we were ready, luck wasn’t on our side. Arctic Adventures denied our request for another slot. No refund, no rescheduling—just money down the drain.
Frustrated, I later checked the booking confirmation—and there it was, in bold, highlighted letters: "Participants must arrive at least 15 minutes before the activity start time."
Of course, we hadn’t read it. And just like that, we paid the price for our ignorance.
The importance of reaching on time was a harsh but valuable lesson we learned that day.
The Silfra Fissure
Since we were already there, we took a small stroll near the pond, soaking in the breathtaking view of the tectonic plates from
outside
By
then, it had started snowing, and we got another yellow alert—not the best weather to stick around. So, we started heading back to Reykjavik.
On the way,
Farini finally snapped—“At least today we’ll eat outside! I’m tired of ready-made food.”
Fair enough. After days of surviving on packed meals, we decided to treat ourselves.
We checked into yet another cozy Airbnb and headed straight to Domino’s.
And guess what?
Two fully loaded pizzas cost us 8,000 INR. Absolutely insane—but totally deserved. 😛
For the first time in days, we did absolutely nothing.
No hikes. No rushing. No itinerary. Just chilling, chatting, and soaking in the local vibes.
And honestly? It was much needed.
As we sat there, unwinding from the chaos of the day,
Cutti suddenly turned to me—“Mattu, what about whale watching? When are we going?”
If Ice Caves and Glacier Hikes were
mine and Rinku’s
must-do activities, then Whale watching was
Cutti’s
ultimate bucket list item.
With a smirk, I looked at her. “Guess we have another adventure left.”
09/12/2024 - The Whale Watching Day
It was
the
much-awaited day for my wife—her eyes sparkled with excitement from the moment she woke up.

We had booked our cruise with Blue Iceland, and honestly, the whole experience was worth every krona we spent. Having been haunted by the ghost of our missed snorkelling slot, we left no room for error this time. We made sure to be on time—no detours, no last-minute coffee cravings, no nothing. Just focused commitment to whales, haha

Once we boarded the massive cruise ship, we grabbed a good spot on the deck, layered up like onions, and braced ourselves for the cold breeze. The sea was calm, the air crisp, and the sky painted in that dull Icelandic gray that somehow makes everything look more dramatic. After about 30 minutes into the ride, the crew pointed at something near the horizon—and suddenly, a massive whale surfaced just a few meters away.

The first glimpse was unreal. A splash and a tail flip, it felt like time paused for a second. There were gasps and cheers all around, but for a moment, we just stood there silently, soaking it all in. Then, as if trying to beat its own performance, another whale popped up on the other side. I swear, it was like they were having a family gathering and we were uninvited guests who got lucky.  For the next hour, we were treated to multiple sightings

After the cruise docked, we were cold, a little wet from the sea mist, but fully satisfied. We headed to our go-to comfort zone—Domino’s (our unofficial trip sponsor at this point)—grabbed some snacks, warmed our hands on the pizza boxes, and laughed through the day’s memories.
Wrapped in layers and smiles, we called it a night, hearts full and bucket lists shorter by one unforgettable experience.
10/12/2024 - The Lagoon

The next day was our visit to the iconic Blue Lagoon—the grand finale of our Icelandic saga. To be honest, we were a bit sceptical about it. Some folks had told us it’s overpriced, overrated, and basically a glorified hot tub. But let me tell you, it’s absolutely one-of-a-kind.

Keeping the cost aside for a moment (which, yes, is expensive), the Blue Lagoon stands apart from every other lagoon in Iceland. While the rest are more like typical hot spring lagoons, this one is uniquely silica-based, giving it that dreamy blue hue and those skincare-promising, Instagram-worthy vibes.

And let's not forget the free drink you get right in the pool. Beer, wine, smoothies—whatever floats your tired traveller soul. Imagine lounging in warm, mineral-rich water, a drink in one hand, face slathered with a white silica mask, and the cold wind just barely kissing your forehead. That kind of convenience and indulgence? Totally worth it.

We spent a good few hours marinating in the pool, pretending we were in a skincare ad, while also clicking the most unhinged, scary-looking pictures imaginable. I finally got a picture with Rinku where both of us looked like zombie snowmen with spa aspirations. A personal win.

But all that bliss came with a small side effect—silica dehydration is real, folks. I started feeling dizzy out of nowhere like I had just walked through a desert in thermal swimwear. Thankfully, I had known beforehand that it’s best to step out the moment dehydration hits. So, I somehow dragged myself out, hardly could take the full shower, grabbed a snack and chugged water like my life depended on it—because honestly, it kind of did at that point.
The Blue Lagoon
I’d say
Blue Lagoon was the perfect way to end the trip
. A spa-like, peaceful, floaty feeling after days of hiking, freezing, and missing activities. It truly felt like the calm after the chaos.
We packed our bags with heavy hearts, as it was our last night in Iceland. The trip was coming to an end, but the memories? Oh, they were just getting warmed up.
11/12/2024 - Final Flickers of Fire & Farewell
Time to wrap up the Iceland trip, and like every good ending, it came with a touch of nostalgia and a whole lot of last-minute scrambling.

We quickly fixed ourselves a breakfast and headed out for some final souvenir hunting. Our first stop? The famous Hallgrímskirkja church. We clicked a few quick photos, grabbed some souvenirs, and took a relaxed stroll through the nearby streets soaking in Reykjavik’s charm one last time.

Then came the unexpected highlight: The Lava Show—Harini’s much-needed bucket list experience. Honestly, when I first heard about it, I rolled my eyes a bit thinking, “It’s molten lava in a man-made setup, how exciting could it be?”
But oh, how wrong I was.
The show turned out to be super insightful and thrilling.
You actually witness real lava flowing—yes, REAL. FLAMING. LAVA, right in front of you, melting rocks, forming silica.
It was not just a visual treat but also a genuinely educational experience. Nature's fury, but in a safe, tourist-friendly setting.
The final picture
We even got a chunk of cooled lava stone as a souvenir. Like, how often do you take a literal piece of Icelandic fire home with you?

And just like that, with a hot stone in our bags and memories hotter than the lava itself, we made our way to the airport, boarded our flight to Venice, and said our final goodbyes to the land of ice and fire.
And that’s a wrap on Iceland. 10/10.
Would freeze, hike, fall, drink, and almost miss activities all over again.
Chasing wonders in Iceland!
